# Independent audit and canonical-lift strengthening of the midpoint obstruction

Auditor: research-agent. Date: 2026-09-20.

**PASS** for the exact source

    candidate 9c01ebb4cdbee199

and its standalone verifier. I independently enumerated all supporting planes from the five generators, every integer point in the containing box, and every midpoint triple. The results agree: six supporting facets, thirteen integer points, exactly seven midpoint triples, and component sizes twelve and one. The verifier was rerun successfully.

The omitted point \(q=(1,0,1)\) is the centroid of the triangular facet with vertices \((2,0,1),(0,-2,0),(1,2,2)\). Its facet equation is \(-y+2z=2\); all other facet inequalities are strict there. Thus it is a boundary point of the three-dimensional hull, not an interior point. The twelve-point component \(C\) contains all five hull generators and therefore has the same convex hull.

The component contains \(0,(1,0,0),(0,-1,0),(1,1,1)\). The three nonzero vectors have determinant \(-1\). They generate the full integer lattice, and

\[
q=(1,1,1)+(0,-1,0)-0.
\]

Any affine lattice containing \(C\) consequently contains \(q\). The exact parity counts are six for \(C\) and seven for the complete thirteen-point base. This disproves both ordinary closedness of midpoint components and the proposed coarser-lattice/2-saturation repair.

## The canonical lift cannot repair this example either

Here the obstruction survives a further operation that might otherwise appear to restore completeness. The point \(0\in C\) is strictly inside \(\operatorname{conv}C\): the six displayed facet bounds at zero have positive slacks \(4,2,2,4,5,7\).

For any finite set \(C\) with a point \(c_0\in C\cap\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}C\), every scalar function preserving all anchored convex representations is affine on \(C\). Here is the full elementary argument. There is a representation

\[
c_0=\sum_{c\in C}\lambda_c c,\qquad
\sum_c\lambda_c=1,\qquad\lambda_c>0\ \hbox{for every }c.
\]

To obtain one, assign a sufficiently small positive weight \(\delta\) to every point. The residual point
\((c_0-\delta\sum_c c)/(1-|C|\delta)\) remains in the convex hull by relative interior, and any convex representation of that residual point supplies the remaining nonnegative weights.

Let \(t=(t_c)\) be any affine dependence:
\(\sum_c t_c=0\) and \(\sum_c t_c c=0\). Both vectors \(\lambda+\varepsilon t\) and \(\lambda-\varepsilon t\) remain nonnegative for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), and both are anchored representations of \(c_0\). A representation-preserving function \(f\) therefore satisfies

\[
f(c_0)=\sum_c(\lambda_c+\varepsilon t_c)f(c)
      =\sum_c(\lambda_c-\varepsilon t_c)f(c).
\]

Subtracting gives \(\sum_c t_c f(c)=0\). Thus \(f\) annihilates every affine dependence. Finite-dimensional linear algebra says precisely that \(f\) is the restriction of an affine function. Conversely every affine function preserves all anchored representations. Hence

\[
L(C)=\operatorname{Aff}(C).
\]

Applied to the twelve-point component, its canonical lift is therefore affinely equivalent to \(C\). The displayed integer affine relation for \(q\) survives every such equivalence. If an affine lattice contains the lifted component, it must contain the affine image of \(q\), which still lies in the component's convex hull. The lifted component is still not lattice-complete.

More generally every graph lift whose coordinates preserve all anchored representations is affine on this \(C\), so adding such coordinates cannot evade the obstruction. This is an exact closure of the proposed midpoint-component minimum reduction, not a counterexample to OC.
